item.title: The Case For Building a Real Estate Tech Stack From the Inside Out
item.dc:creator: Thano Lambrinos
item.description:
Multifamily operators need an independent proptech strategy to control costs, avoid vendor lock-in and build flexible, AI-ready technology stacks.

The post The Case For Building a Real Estate Tech Stack From the Inside Out appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
AI has triggered an unprecedented proliferation of technology solutions. New platforms emerge constantly, each promising to solve operational complexity, reduce cost or unlock competitive advantage. 

The pace of innovation and the pressure to adopt and modernize means that the current corporate real estate system often rewards inertia in the short term. Shiny new offerings often outrun the industry’s ability to evaluate what it is really buying. As a result, too many operators are allowing their strategic technology direction to be steered by vendors selling “solutions,” rather than the people within their businesses who are most familiar with the operational problems that actually need solving.

What makes this pattern so persistent is that the broader ecosystem tends to reinforce it. Consultants recommend familiar products, installers deploy what they know, then service providers maintain existing systems and software platforms for property management, leasing, energy management and more. Refresh cycles bring the same conversations back around. It’s not that anyone in this chain is acting in bad faith; it’s that the incentive structure doesn’t naturally reward asking harder questions about whether a better approach exists.

We’ve seen this play out across the industry with several high-profile proptech companies that raised significant capital, achieve notable valuations and then shifted direction (or went out of business), leaving operators with stranded technology investments and the cost and disruption of replacing infrastructure or software platforms they’d only recently deployed. The pattern isn’t unique to any one company. It reflects a structural gap between how vendors grow and what operators really need.

This pattern is not unique to multifamily either. Across all real estate asset classes, organizations without strong internal technical capabilities consistently cede strategic control to vendors. Over time, this produces rigidity, inflated costs and infrastructure and platforms that are more challenging to evolve as needs change over time.

The operators who will lead the industry long term are those who resist that dynamic. Multifamily is at an inflection point. The challenge is no longer access to tools. It is building the internal capability to evaluate solutions independently, align them to organizational objectives and make decisions grounded in a portfolio’s reality, rather than riding the latest wave of market momentum.

Building a more independent posture requires real investment: in people, in process and in the willingness to take positions that may diverge from prevailing industry practice. That’s not easy, but it’s well worth it in the long run.

Constructing a strong talent foundation is a critical first step. Sometimes the right move is actually looking outside of the multifamily industry, finding engineers and technologists with backgrounds in data centers, hospitals, manufacturing or other sectors where operational complexity is high and the consequences of poor technology management are tangible. These are professionals who have seen what good looks like in other contexts, and who are well-equipped to hold vendor relationships to a high standard, recognizing when a proposed “solution” falls short.

From there, strategy should be developed independently of what the market is selling. That means clearly defining what the organization is seeking to accomplish across its stakeholders – operations teams, residents and investors – before approaching a market that is oversaturated with options. Real estate companies need to tell the market what they need, rather than the other way around.

When building or evaluating a technology stack, the principles that tend to produce durable results are modularity, openness and long-term flexibility. Prioritize open APIs, operator-owned data, infrastructure with long useful lifecycles and systems that integrate cleanly and can evolve without forcing a full rebuild every few years. These are not novel ideas, but they are consistently underweighted when technology decisions are driven by market momentum rather than internal strategy.

The opportunities that follow from this approach are meaningful. Operators who own their technology relationships have more flexibility over cost structure and functionality than those locked into enterprise platforms. Infrastructure decisions — such as deploying passive optical networks rather than defaulting to traditional active copper architectures — can create substantial long term operating advantages that compound over time. Additionally, we find that automation practices more commonly associated with commercial offices can translate more directly into residential environments than the industry has historically assumed.

None of this requires proprietary technology breakthroughs. It requires the right people, a clear strategy and the discipline to evaluate technology decisions from the inside out.

It has never been more important to be in control of a tech stack than in the wake of unprecedented AI disruption. Operators are making significant commitments to AI vendors at a moment when the landscape is still evolving and business models are still being tested. This choice is popular now, but it’s riskier than it might appear on the surface.

After all, popularity in the market and fit for every portfolio’s strategy are two very different things. The most important discipline in proptech right now is knowing the difference.

item.title: Six Regional MLSs File Joint Lawsuit to Block Compass Policy Challenge
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Six regional MLSs sue Compass in New York federal court seeking to uphold listing cooperation rules and block threatened litigation over pre-marketing policies.

The post Six Regional MLSs File Joint Lawsuit to Block Compass Policy Challenge appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Arizona Regional MLS, BridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS, Hive MLS, and REcolorado filed a joint lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 21 in the Southern District of New York. The six organizations, which represent more than 120,000 real estate professionals, seek a declaratory judgment that their cooperation rules comply with federal and state antitrust laws. The suit also requests a permanent injunction barring Compass from suing any of the six MLSs over their listing submission and pre-marketing policies. The action follows demand letters Compass sent to MLSs in September threatening litigation against any organization that fines agents who violate listing rules.

Compass sent letters demanding that MLSs allow brokers to market listings publicly without submitting them to the cooperative database. The brokerage argues homesellers should control how their property is marketed without agents facing fines. The six MLSs counter that Compass wants to access MLS data for its buyer clients while withholding its own listings, a practice they characterize as free riding that undermines the cooperative model. Greg Skidmore, representing the plaintiffs, said the rules ensure transparency and broad access to timely listing information. Compass pointed to several MLSs across 12 states that currently permit public marketing without MLS submission.

The complaint alleges Compass aims to use its inventory as leverage to drive smaller brokerages out of business, reducing competition and consumer choice. California Regional MLS filed a separate lawsuit against Compass on Oct. 5 after receiving a similar demand letter. Compass countersued CRMLS less than a week later, alleging the MLS enforces competition-blocking rules through fines, suspensions, and expulsions. Rocket Companies, which partnered with Compass earlier this year, co-signed an open letter in March accusing certain MLSs of working against member agents. Other large MLSs including Unlock MLS and OneKey MLS have issued public responses defending their listing policies.

item.title: Rent Payment Platforms Face Legal Challenge Over Undisclosed Transaction Fees
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Baltimore sues property manager and rent payment platforms over undisclosed transaction fees charged to low-income tenants through electronic payment systems.

The post Rent Payment Platforms Face Legal Challenge Over Undisclosed Transaction Fees appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore’s city solicitor filed suit against Pennrose Management Company, RentCafe, and Yardi Systems, alleging they charged tenants undisclosed fees for electronic rent payments that violate Maryland consumer protection law. Tenants at nine Pennrose-operated low-income housing developments faced annual service fees of $300 to $420 when paying by credit or debit card through the RentCafe platform, according to the complaint filed in Baltimore Circuit Court. Pennrose switched to mandatory electronic payments in 2024, eliminating in-person rent collection. A free automatic payment option exists but requires a bank account, which many low-income tenants lack.

Rents at Pennrose properties range from $869 for one-bedroom units to $1,654 for four-bedroom apartments, housing primarily older adults, people with disabilities, and residents on fixed incomes. The lawsuit argues tenants received no additional services in exchange for the fees but risked eviction if they refused to pay. City Solicitor Ebony Thompson said renters should not have to navigate unclear charges to understand their payment obligations. Representatives for all three defendants did not respond to requests for comment.

Baltimore renter households paying more than they can afford for rent and utilities account for roughly 40 percent of the city’s rental market, with very low-income renters facing the most acute burden. A 2024 lawsuit filed by Baltimore resident Rodney Deaver against his landlord over similar charges resulted in a judgment exceeding $250,000, roughly 800 times what the defendants acknowledged owing. Baltimore Circuit Judge Catherine Chen justified that award based on the inconvenience and dismissiveness Deaver encountered. Organizations in neighboring Howard County, Maryland have begun warning tenants about mandatory fees for trash valet services, parking permits, and other charges residents cannot decline.

The Baltimore Banner
Baltimore Sues Property Manager, Software Vendors for Charging ‘Junk Fees’

The post Rent Payment Platforms Face Legal Challenge Over Undisclosed Transaction Fees appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Yardi Picks Up the Rent Pricing Fight Where RealPage Left Off
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Private plaintiffs are pursuing treble damages

The post Yardi Picks Up the Rent Pricing Fight Where RealPage Left Off appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
2 days 19 hr agoOct. 21, 2026 2:03 pm

While the antitrust fight over RealPage has dominated attention, a quieter case against Yardi Systems, Inc. has been working its way through federal court in Seattle for three years, and it just took a turn that could make it the more consequential of the two. A Washington renter named McKenna Duffy sued Yardi and a group of property managers in September 2023, alleging that they used the software now called Revenue IQ, formerly RENTmaximizer, to coordinate rents across competing properties by routing non-public pricing data through a common algorithm. The proposed class covers leases dating back to September 8, 2019. On October 13, Judge Robert S. Lasnik of the US District Court for the Western District of Washington denied Yardi’s motion for summary judgment and lifted a stay that had kept plaintiffs from taking discovery against the landlords named alongside it.

Plaintiffs advance three theories in the operative complaint. The first is a hub-and-spoke conspiracy in which each landlord agreed with Yardi to use the product and the landlords agreed horizontally among themselves to inflate rents. The third alleges that defendants used Yardi as a conduit to exchange timely, competitively sensitive, non-public information. A second theory alleging unlawful vertical restraints was abandoned, and the court granted summary judgment on that count.

Yardi had persuaded the court in March 2025 to split discovery, confining the first phase to its own products on the theory that examining how the software actually works might resolve the case without dragging in the landlords. That phase closed in November 2025, and Yardi moved for summary judgment on the strength of it, pointing to individualized software configurations, client-selected reference rents, clients’ ability to modify or reject recommendations, and the absence of any direct use of one client’s confidential information in computing another client’s output. Lasnik found the approach insufficient because the arguments reached beyond the technology, noting that Yardi was asking him to draw inferences about the landlord defendants’ knowledge, communications, and conduct, including whether their use of the product reflected independent decisionmaking. The purpose of phasing, he wrote, was to determine whether Yardi-focused discovery could obviate broader discovery. “It has not.”

The parallels to RealPage, Inc. are close enough that the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission filed a Statement of Interest in the Yardi case in March 2024, arguing that landlords retaining some pricing discretion does not defeat a price-fixing claim. Both cases describe a software vendor collecting non-public data from competing landlords, feeding pricing recommendations back to them, and hosting user conferences where competitors discussed strategy. Both rest on the proposition that a cartel does not require the members to talk to each other if they are all talking to the same algorithm.

Where the two diverge is in who is prosecuting. RealPage faced the DOJ, nine state attorneys general, and private plaintiffs at once, and the government case ended in a consent decree filed November 24, 2025 that carried no financial penalty and no admission of wrongdoing. RealPage agreed to stop using competitors’ non-public data at runtime and in model training, to limit itself to data at least twelve months old and not drawn from active leases, to redesign features that limit price decreases or align pricing, to stop reporting pricing data more granularly than statewide, and to accept a court-appointed monitor with access to its source code and runtime logic for up to seven years. The money came from elsewhere. Greystar settled a private class action for $50 million in October 2025 and paid $7 million to nine state attorneys general the following month.

Yardi is privately held and faces no government enforcement action at present, only a Statement of Interest that carries no remedy of its own. That cuts both ways. There is no DOJ on the other side of the table offering a no-penalty consent decree, and private plaintiffs under the Clayton Act are seeking treble damages across a class period now in its seventh year. The RealPage decree suggests what injunctive relief tends to look like in these matters, which is restrictions on data vintage and granularity, feature redesigns, and a monitor. It says considerably less about exposure in a case where the only parties at the table want money.

What happens next depends on a record that does not exist yet. Discovery against the landlord defendants is only now beginning, the expert motions on both sides were denied without prejudice because they were briefed on an incomplete record, and the parties have 28 days to propose a plan for the remainder. Yardi may renew its summary judgment motion once that is done, and Lasnik was explicit that his order expresses no view on the merits of its arguments. We would expect the landlord communications to determine the outcome more than the source code does, which is roughly what the DOJ argued two and a half years ago.

item.title: Vacant Urban Retail Finds Second Life in AI Infrastructure Demand
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A Maryland firm wants to turn San Francisco's vacant Centre mall into an AI data center, competing with retail and sports proposals.

The post Vacant Urban Retail Finds Second Life in AI Infrastructure Demand appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
KG Growth Partners, a Maryland-based financial advisory firm, filed a permit inquiry in June to convert a 350,000-square-foot portion of San Francisco’s shuttered Centre mall into an AI data center. The firm is working with an unnamed partner interested in the former Bloomingdale’s space. KG’s CEO Jared Kreiger told the San Francisco Chronicle the project would keep ground floors active and open while reserving upper floors for technical use, partnering with a known AI lab to create AI-controlled living space with features like rooftop gardens for nonprofit food programs.

The inquiry arrived just as Mayor Daniel Lurie signed a 45-day moratorium on new data center approvals, directing the planning department to study their impacts. San Francisco Centre closed in January 2026 after Nordstrom and Bloomingdale’s both exited in 2025, leaving high vacancy. Presidio Bay Ventures and Prado Group had planned a retail and commercial conversion but walked away in July over ground lease negotiations. Other proposals have included a soccer stadium and a multi-level sports complex with a members-only club.

The data center pitch reflects growing competition for urban real estate between traditional uses and AI infrastructure. Developers nationwide are repurposing vacant retail, industrial, and even office buildings to meet surging demand for computing capacity near population centers. Power and cooling requirements make these conversions complex, but the premium rents data center operators pay can exceed what struggling retail centers generate. San Francisco’s moratorium suggests cities are beginning to weigh infrastructure needs against neighborhood impacts as AI firms chase scarce urban sites.

San Francisco’s Doomed Mall Probed as Future Data Center

item.title: Big Office Tenants Are Running Out of Places to Go
item.dc:creator: Travis Barrington
item.description:
U.S. office availability is falling as construction stalls, leaving large tenants competing for scarce Class A, trophy and flexible space.

The post Big Office Tenants Are Running Out of Places to Go appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
For years the office story was about too much space. The third-quarter numbers suggest the more pressing problem, at least at the top of the market, is too little of the right kind.

Savills’ Q3 2026 market reports show availability falling year over year in 21 of the 24 U.S. markets it tracks. Manhattan’s rate is down 280 basis points, San Francisco’s down 640. At the same time, the pipeline of new buildings has almost vanished. Cushman & Wakefield puts the Americas construction pipeline 82% below its 2020 peak, and Atlanta has no office projects under construction for the first time in 15 years. Tenants with big requirements are discovering that a market with 25% availability can still have very few good buildings with a contiguous 50,000 square feet to offer.

The pipeline has nearly run dry

The supply side of the story is stark. Cushman & Wakefield’s Global Trends in Flexible Office 2026 report puts the Americas office construction pipeline at just under 32 million square feet. That is an 82% drop from its recent peak of 175 million square feet in the first quarter of 2020.

With so little new product coming, occupiers and owners are improvising. Flexible office inventory in the U.S. grew 18% year over year as of Q2 2026, and flex space now makes up 3.1% of total national office inventory, up from 2.6% a year earlier and 2.3% in 2024. All 25 of the largest U.S. flex markets added inventory, and suburban flex locations grew 39% between 2024 and 2026, compared with 22% for urban ones. Leasing by the largest flex providers over the past four quarters ran 32% above 2021 to 2023 levels.

Cushman’s researchers frame flex less as a stopgap and more as part of the market’s permanent plumbing: a faster path to quality space for tenants, and a tool landlords are using to fill underused floors as part of broader repositioning.

The 50,000-square-foot problem

Headline availability rates across most markets remain above 20%, which makes the market look roomy. Savills argues that for big tenants it is anything but. Its Q3 Office Spotlight finds that across 16 North American markets, an average of 12.2% of office buildings can offer a contiguous block of 50,000 square feet or more. Then Savills narrows the pool. With each filter, the options shrink sharply: 11.5% once buildings with distressed owners are removed, 7.0% for Class A only, and 3.3% for Class A in each market’s three strongest submarkets. Just 0.6% of buildings are trophy properties with a large block available. Savills’ summary: the challenge for large occupiers is no longer finding available space, it’s finding the right space.

Manhattan shows the squeeze clearly. Some 13.4% of its buildings have a large block, but only 1.0% are Class A buildings in its top three submarkets, and none are trophy towers. Dallas-Fort Worth falls from 14.4% to 0.1% at the trophy level, and Silicon Valley, Miami and Montréal have no trophy options at all. Miami starts with the thinnest supply, just 2.4% of buildings, and its city report counts only ten blocks of 50,000 to 100,000 square feet and two above 100,000. Downtown Chicago has the most large blocks, 32.1% of buildings, but Savills notes much of that space sits in older stock that increasingly needs conversion. Washington, D.C. holds up best at the top, with 8.1% of buildings offering a large Class A block in its best submarkets.

Savills expects premium availability to tighten further, because the depleted development pipeline is years away from delivering meaningful new options. Its advice to occupiers is blunt: start the search earlier, because fewer viable blocks mean longer decision timelines and stiffer competition.

Where the market is tightening

Manhattan is the clearest case of demand outrunning supply. Savills counted 10.3 million square feet of leasing in Q3, slightly below Q2 but still above the 2015 to 2019 quarterly average, and year-to-date volume is up 5.6% to 33.5 million square feet. Availability fell 280 basis points from a year earlier to 13.4%, sublease space shrank from 12.4 million to 8.9 million square feet, and average asking rents rose 8.9% to $82.14 per square foot. Class A rents climbed 9.9% to $94.91.

The deals were large and concentrated in tech, media and law. Proskauer Rose renewed and expanded to 478,000 square feet at 11 Times Square, Anthropic committed to 465,630 square feet at 330 Hudson Street, and Havas Health took 254,118 square feet at 200 Madison Avenue. Seven other leases topped 150,000 square feet. Meanwhile Manhattan’s office inventory has shrunk by 7.4 million square feet in a year as buildings leave the stock.

Dallas-Fort Worth posted the fastest rent growth of the 24 U.S. markets in Savills’ Q3 reports. Average asking rents there rose 9.7%, and Class A rents jumped 12.5% to $44.06, with Class A capturing 74% of leasing. Morgan Stanley’s planned 700,000-square-foot move into a new Uptown tower in 2031 is the anchor of what Savills calls the region’s financial-services boom.

Atlanta shows what happens when the cranes stop entirely. With 1072 West Peachtree delivered, the metro has no office projects under construction for the first time in 15 years. Availability fell 140 basis points to 26.1%, Class A drove nearly two-thirds of leasing, and trophy rents are approaching $70 per square foot.

The same pattern runs through other markets. Downtown Chicago hit a record average asking rent of $48.88, with Class A availability down 180 basis points to 22.2% as inventory shrank by 3.2 million square feet. Austin’s availability has declined for six straight quarters, to 24.0%. Charlotte’s availability is down 400 basis points from a year ago, and a newly delivered tower there opened fully leased at rents above $65 per square foot.

Where it is still loose

Not every market is tightening, and the averages often hide a two-speed recovery. San Diego leasing fell 20.7% from Q2 to 1.0 million square feet, availability ticked up 40 basis points to 21.0%, and average asking rents slipped 2.0% to $3.61 per square foot per month. Downtown availability reached 35.8%, though Savills attributes the jump to roughly 2.7 million square feet of obsolete buildings being reclassified, not to tenants leaving.

Denver’s numbers show the same split inside one metro. Leasing hit a multiyear high on big aerospace renewals, but CBD availability sits at 42.0% while Cherry Creek is at 13.4%. In Houston, leasing ran 11.8% below the five-year quarterly average and overall rents rose less than 1%. Yet trophy and premier Class A availability there is just 12.7%, less than half the overall rate of 26.2%.

Los Angeles posted its strongest leasing since 2019 at 4.0 million square feet, largely on renewals. Even so, availability remains 26.5%, and Savills notes concessions near historic highs are holding effective rents down. Philadelphia’s report uses the phrase “K-shaped” to describe a recovery where the best buildings pull away and the rest wait.

San Francisco, long the cautionary tale, is now a recovery story. Leasing is on pace for one of its best years in decades, with 12.1 million square feet signed through Q3 versus 8.1 million a year earlier. Availability dropped 640 basis points in a year to 27.2%. AI and tech firms are the main drivers, and Savills reports that large blocks of trophy space are already limited.

The ripple reaches Class B

Savills expects the squeeze at the top to push demand down the quality ladder, toward well-located buildings with financially stable owners that sit a notch below trophy status. New York offers an early read on what that looks like.

The Real Estate Board of New York tracked 200 Class B office buildings in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens and found average visitation has settled at 72% of pre-pandemic levels. The average hides a wide spread. One in five buildings is now busier than before the pandemic and another 21% are between 80% and 100%, while 32% remain at or below half.

Location matters. Midtown Class B buildings hit 89% of pre-pandemic visitation in August, compared with roughly 70% in Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn/Queens. REBNY points to experienced ownership, transit access and a diversified tenant roster as the dividing lines, with big single-tenant vacancies and coworking pullbacks dragging down the weakest buildings. The group also credits tightening Class A availability for helping Class B, which is exactly the spillover Savills is forecasting nationally.

What comes next

For occupiers, the practical message from these reports is timing. Large tenants in tight submarkets should expect fewer options, longer searches and less negotiating room at the top of the market. Many are responding by renewing in place: renewals made up more than half of the largest deals in Downtown Chicago and 60% of the top deals in Los Angeles, and Google renewed nearly 1.6 million square feet at Moffett Place in Sunnyvale.

For owners, the gap is widening between buildings that can capture that demand and those that cannot. Well-located Class A and upgraded Class B assets with stable ownership stand to gain pricing power. Obsolete stock keeps leaving the market through conversion and demolition, which is helping pull down availability in Manhattan, Chicago, Boston and Northern Virginia. With almost nothing new under construction, the next real test is how soon rents at the top rise far enough to justify building again.

item.title: Tiny Apartments, Massive Amenities: How Seattle’s 1,131-Unit Tower Bets on Luxury Living
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Seattle House's 1,131 units open in November with below-average unit sizes, premium rents, and 50,000 square feet of hotel-style amenities near Amazon headquarters.

The post Tiny Apartments, Massive Amenities: How Seattle’s 1,131-Unit Tower Bets on Luxury Living appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Seattle House, a 1,131-unit development near Amazon’s headquarters, opens to its first tenants on November 15 after seven years of construction. Developed by Vancouver, British Columbia-based Concord Pacific and Seattle-based HB Management, the $371 million project features two 45-story towers connected by a 13-story podium across a half-block site. General manager Nathan Leible reported more than 200 tours and over 50 signed leases in the first four weekends of showings, though he declined to share overall occupancy rates.

Units run smaller than national averages, matching Seattle’s position as the city with the smallest new apartments in the country at 645 square feet on average. Monthly rents start at $2,200 for a studio, $2,600 for a one-bedroom, and $4,100 for a two-bedroom, topping out at $7,200 for a two-bedroom unit just under 1,000 square feet on the top floor. Tenants trade floor space for access to more than 50,000 square feet of amenities including an outdoor infinity pool, a large gym with steam room and sauna, a dog spa roughly double the size of a small studio, and a second-floor co-working area with five phone rooms, five meeting rooms, and a coffee bar.

Construction began in 2019 but faced years of delays from the pandemic, a street-use permit dispute, and a concrete truck driver strike that paused work for more than a year. Seattle House joins several other large apartment projects in the area, including a neighboring 45-story tower by Holland Partner Group and NASH and a two-tower project by Vancouver’s Onni Group. Centreville Construction served as general contractor, with Arcadis as architect and Avenue5 Residential handling property management.

item.title: CBRE’s Billion-Dollar Bet Follows Data Center Boom Inside the Racks
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
CBRE's $1 billion Onnec acquisition adds data center cabling and equipment installation to its traditional services as AI spending reshapes the sector.

The post CBRE’s Billion-Dollar Bet Follows Data Center Boom Inside the Racks appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
CBRE agreed to acquire London-based Onnec Group for roughly $610 million in cash plus up to $400 million in performance-based payments. Onnec employs 800 people who install and maintain cabling and equipment racks inside data centers for major technology clients across Europe and Asia Pacific. Combined with CBRE’s 2024 purchase of U.S.-based Direct Line, the deal shifts the firm’s data center business from traditional construction and brokerage services into the technical infrastructure where servers operate. Chief Executive Bob Sulentic said the moves take CBRE into “where the actual compute happens.”

Data center capacity in eight major U.S. markets grew nearly 34% in the year ended June 30, with vacancy at just 1.4%. Infrastructure work, including data centers, energy, and transportation, now generates 14% of CBRE’s earnings, up from 3% in 2021. The firm expects roughly $7 billion in infrastructure revenue by 2027. JLL, the second-largest commercial real estate services firm, has also expanded its data center team, roughly doubling headcount over the past two years.

The expansion ties commercial real estate firms more closely to technology spending cycles, raising questions about concentration risk. Sulentic acknowledged the AI and data center market is “extremely frothy,” though he pointed to revenue opportunities beyond new construction, including facility upgrades and management. Shares of CBRE, JLL, and other services firms fell sharply in February as investors weighed whether AI could automate research, valuations, and dealmaking functions. JPMorgan analyst Anthony Paolone called fears of AI replacing brokers overblown, citing the complexity of negotiations and due diligence.

Real-Estate Giant CBRE Gets Deeper Into Data Centers With $1 Billion Deal

item.title: Investors Push Back on H&R REIT Breakup Over What the CEO’s Family Is Paying
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Analysts estimate a potential C$500 million valuation gap

The post Investors Push Back on H&R REIT Breakup Over What the CEO’s Family Is Paying appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
4 days 13 hr agoOct. 19, 2026 7:45 pm

Toronto-based H&R Real Estate Investment Trust is losing support for a breakup and sale agreement it signed in August, as a widening group of institutional holders objects to the share of value going to assets controlled by the family of its chief executive. The transaction would split the company apart, sending the industrial portfolio to Blackstone Inc. and a group of co-investors while New York-based GO Residential Real Estate Investment Trust takes the residential assets, most of them in the US sunbelt. Stockholders would receive a combination of cash and GO shares. A separate company called CRAL, controlled by the family of executive chairman and chief executive Tom Hofstedter, would acquire roughly C$2 billion worth of properties from H&R, and the price it is paying for them has become the central issue ahead of a November 13 vote.

Analysts at RBC Capital Markets estimated that CRAL is paying about C$500 million less than the properties it would receive are worth, while cautioning that many of those assets are hard to sell and carry substantial potential liabilities. They have also questioned whether H&R’s decision to pursue a single transaction for the whole company cost unitholders a better outcome, writing last week that he struggles to see how they approve the deal.

Opposition has accumulated steadily since H&R disclosed details of a sale process that ran nearly two years and included earlier cash offers that ultimately collapsed. Sandpiper Group, which holds 1 percent of the shares, said Friday it would vote against and has retained Norton Rose Fulbright Canada LLP as legal counsel alongside Kingsdale Advisors. Scheer, Rowlett & Associates Investment Management Ltd. followed on Monday, with Toronto-based portfolio manager Brenna Phelan confirming in a statement that a large shareholder intends to vote against the proposed transaction.

Market movement since August has not helped the case. The offer was initially worth C$12.01 per share and valued H&R at C$6.7 billion on an enterprise basis. GO REIT units have since fallen, pulling the implied value to roughly C$10.50, while H&R itself traded at C$9.81 Monday afternoon in Toronto. Approval requires two-thirds of all votes cast and a separate majority of votes cast by minority investors, a structure built for transactions where insiders sit on both sides.

H&R’s trustees may be right that no better offer for the whole company existed, and the properties going to CRAL do appear to be the ones that stalled the broader sale. A controlling family willing to take difficult assets off the table is arguably doing the rest of the shareholders a favor, but only if the discount attached to that willingness is the right size. The two-year process H&R disclosed was meant to establish an accurate valuation. What it seems to have established instead is how few buyers were interested, which is a weaker form of proof than it looked like in August. The November vote will come down to whether minority holders believe that the cost of the assets is at least close to what they would get for them in a very slow market.

item.title: Lack of Service Coordination Drives Buyer Frustration in Residential Deals
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A HomeServices survey shows 70% of buyers found homebuying a hassle, with uncoordinated providers driving frustration and demand for agent-led coordination.

The post Lack of Service Coordination Drives Buyer Frustration in Residential Deals appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A HomeServices of America survey of 1,000 recent homebuyers found that nearly 70% described the homebuying transaction as a hassle. Uncoordinated service providers—real estate agents, mortgage lenders, insurance providers, and title companies—accounted for 46% of buyer frustration. Nearly seven in 10 buyers entered the process expecting their real estate agent to play a role in coordinating mortgage, title, and insurance services. The research indicates that increased access to digital tools has not simplified the transaction for most consumers.

Buyers report that changes in financing, insurance issues, and title questions create cascading delays when providers operate independently. HomeServices found that 79% of respondents would prefer an integrated system for mortgage, title, and insurance coordinated by their real estate agent if they were to purchase again. The company’s OnePoint solution bundles real estate, mortgage, title, and insurance services while keeping the agent at the center of the transaction. Only about one-quarter of respondents preferred an app-driven experience with minimal human interaction; the majority favored people-led transactions supported by technology.

Brokerages have focused on digitizing individual transaction components, but the survey points to coordination as the next competitive differentiator. Real estate professionals are increasingly serving as central points of communication, connecting buyers with trusted providers and managing interdependent deadlines. Integrated service models are emerging as a response to consumer demand for simplified workflows without removing personal guidance from high-stakes decisions. Buyers want visibility and communication, but they still expect a professional to put information into context throughout the transaction.
